extracted.intended_audience: patent prosecutors (U.S.) — patent attorneys and agents drafting and prosecuting applications
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for drafting patent specifications and prosecuting U.S. patent applications to produce broad, enforceable claims while avoiding common pitfalls (e.g., admissions, inequitable conduct, harmful amendments, prior-art mistakes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prosecute claims of appropriate scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Prosecute claims of sufficient scope to read on the competition, yet just narrow enough to avoid the prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance claim breadth against prior art; aim to capture competitors' implementations while remaining patentable. Craft multiple claim scopes (broad independent, narrower fallbacks) so that at least some claims survive prior-art attacks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide full written description support
rubrics_metrics.description: Fully describe the inventor’s conception to provide support for the broadest claim construction possible and to comply with the requirements of various written description laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include general descriptions as well as specific embodiments so the specification supports broad functional claim language; avoid limiting the disclosure to narrow examples only; ensure the specification permits the claimed scope under §112/written description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obtain strong, enforceable claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Obtain strong, enforceable claims that will withstand validity challenges and be difficult to design around to achieve non-infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft claims to be defensible in validity fights and to reduce easy design-arounds (e.g., functional claim drafting, multiple claim formats, careful fallback claim sets). Consider enforceability risks from prosecution history and specification statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent’s own words can restrict claim scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Statements in the specification and prosecution history that would have no impact in other jurisdictions may narrow claim scope in the U.S.; the specification is the single best guide to the meaning of a disputed term (Phillips v. AWH).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid language in the specification or arguments that will be used to limit claim terms during claim construction. Be mindful that how terms are described or exemplified in the spec can be used to construe claims narrowly in litigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid troublesome specification drafting practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Several drafting habits can inadvertently narrow claims or create problems: vague claim terms with corresponding narrow disclosure; inconsistent use of terms; highlighting non-claimed features of embodiments; narrow examples without a more general description; describing unclaimed benefits; attributing the word 'invention' to unclaimed features; ordinary words may be limiting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure consistent terminology throughout the application; accompany examples with broader descriptions; avoid emphasizing only narrow aspects or non-claimed features; do not call unclaimed features 'the invention.' Use generic language to support broader constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be precise and consistent in wording and definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Word choice (e.g., 'at' vs. 'to', 'is' vs. 'may be', 'the invention is' vs. 'the invention may include') can determine claim scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define claim terms broadly and consistently; where appropriate use functional language, ranges, and examples rather than absolute definitive statements. Carefully review specification wording to avoid inadvertent limitations (illustrated by Chef America v. Lamb-Weston where 'to' vs 'at' affected claim construction).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid 'patent profanity' in specification and prosecution
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid using suggestive limiting adjectives or labels (e.g., 'peculiar', 'significant', 'critical', 'special', 'essential', 'key', 'necessary', 'preferable (?)') that may be interpreted as limitations on the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not label features as 'essential' or 'critical' unless you intend to limit the claim to those features; prefer neutral descriptions and functional embodiments that preserve flexibility in claim interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid unnecessary amendments and arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: Unnecessary amendments and/or arguments may create potential estoppels and narrow claim scope; amendments for patentability can surrender claim scope and equivalents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the Examiner bear the burden of rejection. In the first response, attack the basis of the rejection rather than immediately amending. If amendment is necessary, be surgical and preserve the most valuable embodiments; keep arguments concise and focused to avoid creating estoppels in prosecution history.

rubrics_metrics.name: First response strategy: attack the rejection premise
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer attacking the premise/basis of an obviousness rejection over amending claims to avoid prosecution-history estoppel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus arguments on flaws in the Examiner’s reliance on prior art (e.g., lack of suggestion/motivation, no reasonable expectation of success). Reserve amendments for a second, carefully crafted response if necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use unpredictability and reasonable-expectation arguments against obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Emphasize unpredictability and lack of reasonable expectation of success to counter obviousness rejections (per KSR and USPTO guidelines).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argue that combining or substituting known elements would not have yielded predictable results; resist 'obvious to try' rationales if a finite number of predictable solutions with expectation of success is absent. Use technical facts about unpredictability to rebut KSR rationales (such as simple substitution, known techniques yielding predictable results, or cross-field promptings).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider industry-specific predictability differences
rubrics_metrics.description: The level of predictability differs by art: chem/bio are often characterized as unpredictable, while mechanical/electrical arts are more predictable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tailor obviousness/enablement arguments to the field; in unpredictable arts emphasize lack of reasonable expectation of success; in predictable arts recognize that obviousness may be easier to show and plan claim strategies accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surrendering equivalents / doctrine of equivalents risk
rubrics_metrics.description: Narrowing amendments made for patentability create a presumption that equivalents for the narrowed element were surrendered (prosecution-history estoppel), which can limit ability to rely on the doctrine of equivalents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid or minimize narrowing amendments when possible; if necessary, preserve equivalents by careful claim drafting, dependent claims, and by framing arguments to avoid broad concessions. Be aware that literal claim scope, specification, prosecution history, amendments, arguments, and §112 issues all interplay with DOE analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior art awareness and search quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Most patents fail during enforcement based on prior art newly discovered after the patent issues; being unaware or ill-informed about prior art weakens enforcement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perform robust prior-art searches (including your own files and nonobvious places) before filing to craft claims that avoid known art. Do not view prior art through rose-colored glasses; build fallback positions and dependent-claim strategies so that if one claim falls others survive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid admissions about prior art in specification or prosecution
rubrics_metrics.description: Statements in the application that something is prior art (or headings like 'Description of Prior Art') are binding for determinations of anticipation and obviousness; IDS admissions can likewise be binding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not call something 'prior art' in the specification or unnecessary prosecution paperwork. Avoid overt admissions in the spec or IDS; if prior art must be discussed, do so neutrally and carefully to avoid binding characterizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid mischaracterization of results/facts; duty of disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants (inventors and attorneys) have an obligation to inform the Patent Office of information that might affect patentability; mischaracterization or omission of material information with intent can constitute inequitable conduct and render the entire patent unenforceable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure all material information is disclosed and that statements are truthful. Be conservative in representations about experimental results, comparative data, and the inventors' own publications. Maintain contemporaneous documentation supporting statements made during prosecution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inequitable conduct elements to avoid
rubrics_metrics.description: Inequitable conduct exists if the applicant (1) failed to disclose material information, (2) submitted false material information, or (3) made an affirmative misrepresentation of a material fact — together with intent to deceive the USPTO.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat materiality and intent carefully: disclose information that a reasonable examiner would consider important; avoid misstatements; do not withhold known adverse information. Intent to deceive is required for inequitable conduct findings — be scrupulous in disclosures and IDS handling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure examples and experimental statements are accurate and supported
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples written in the past tense suggest the work was done; using examples relied on for patentability increases scrutiny.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify with inventors whether experiments were actually performed before filing. Check that examples correctly reflect what was done, confirm any comparative data are statistically significant, and search for inventor publications or other statements inconsistent with the examples. Use Rule 132 declarations where appropriate to support factual claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim-drafting tactics: use multiple tiers, dependent claims, and alternative independent claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Craft multiple tiers of claim strategies so that if one falls you have backups; use dependent claims effectively and consider additional independent claims to recite subject matter alternatively to avoid the prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design claim sets with layered fallback positions (broad → intermediate → narrow). If amending, preserve alternative claim paths (e.g., different independent claim formats) to reduce the risk that a single amendment or rejection will destroy all enforceable scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prosecution argument style: concise, focused, and prior-art-focused
rubrics_metrics.description: When arguing, concentrate on the Examiner’s prior-art rationale and be concise and focused to avoid making unnecessary concessions that narrow claim scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid extended narrative about the invention itself when responding to rejections; instead, dissect the Examiner's cited references and explain why they do not teach/modify/combine to yield the claimed invention. Keep arguments technical and prior-art-centric.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid overreaching obviousness rebuttals that create enablement problems
rubrics_metrics.description: When rebutting obviousness, do not overemphasize how difficult it would be to make the modification suggested by the Examiner in a way that later undermines enablement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strike a balance: present enough evidence of unpredictability or lack of reasonable expectation of success to defeat obviousness without asserting claims about enablement that could be used against you later. Establish an appropriate level of ordinary skill in the art consistent with both obviousness and enablement positions.
